jurisdictions.title: Pennsylvania (US-PA)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. Pennsylvania bans standing *on a roadway* to solicit a ride. The legal definition of "roadway" excludes the shoulder and berm, so thumbing from the shoulder or sidewalk is not covered by that rule. The Pennsylvania Turnpike is different: hitchhiking and all pedestrian entry onto the Turnpike right-of-way are banned there by regulation.

sections.summary:
The Vehicle Code (75 Pa.C.S. § 3545) follows the standard Uniform Vehicle Code pattern: "No person shall [...] Stand on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride." Section 102 defines "roadway" as the part of the highway used for vehicle travel, "exclusive of the sidewalk, berm or shoulder." So the statewide rule reaches people standing in the travel lanes, not people standing on the shoulder or sidewalk.

What still applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stay out of the travel lanes.** Stand on the shoulder, berm or sidewalk, and pick a spot where a driver can pull completely off the road.
- **The Pennsylvania Turnpike is off limits.** Turnpike Commission regulations prohibit hitchhiking and prohibit pedestrians from entering the Turnpike right-of-way at all, and they also prohibit drivers from stopping to let hitchhikers board. Ask for rides on a local road before the Turnpike entrance, not on the Turnpike itself.
- **Other freeways:** The Vehicle Code does not contain a blanket statutory ban on pedestrians on freeways. Instead, § 3313 lets PennDOT prohibit any "class or kind of traffic" on a limited access highway and requires it to post signs at the entrances; once signs are posted, disobeying them is a violation. In practice most interstate ramps carry signs barring pedestrians, so treat a signed ramp as closed to you.
- **Walk on the sidewalk** if there is one; otherwise on the shoulder; otherwise on the left edge facing traffic (§ 3544).

A violation of § 3545 is a summary offense with a $25 fine under § 6502. A Turnpike regulation violation is also a summary offense with a $25 fine.
sections.laws:
### 75 Pa.C.S. § 3545: Pedestrians soliciting rides or business

**Source:** [Pennsylvania General Assembly, 75 Pa.C.S. § 3545](https://www.palegis.us/statutes/consolidated/view-statute?txtType=HTM&ttl=75&div=0&chapter=35&section=45&subsctn=0)

> No person shall:
>
> (1) Stand on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride.
>
> (2) Stand on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting employment, business or contributions from the occupant of any vehicle.
>
> (3) Stand on or in proximity to a highway for the purpose of soliciting the watching or guarding of any vehicle while parked or about to be parked on a street or highway.

**What it means:** You may not stand in the part of the road cars drive on to ask for a ride. The rule says "roadway," not "highway," so standing on the shoulder or sidewalk is not covered (see the definition below).

### 75 Pa.C.S. § 102: Definitions ("Roadway", "Highway", "Limited access highway", "Freeway")

**Source:** [Pennsylvania General Assembly, 75 Pa.C.S. § 102](https://www.palegis.us/statutes/consolidated/view-statute?txtType=HTM&ttl=75&div=0&chapter=1&section=2&subsctn=0)

> "Freeway." A limited access highway to which the only means of ingress and egress is by interchange ramps.
>
> [...]
>
> "Highway." The entire width between the boundary lines of every way publicly maintained when any part thereof is open to the use of the public for purposes of vehicular travel. [...]
>
> [...]
>
> "Limited access highway." A highway in respect to which owners or occupants of abutting lands and other persons have no legal right of access except at points and in the manner determined by the authority having jurisdiction over the highway.
>
> [...]
>
> "Roadway." That portion of a highway improved, designed or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the sidewalk, berm or shoulder even though such sidewalk, berm or shoulder is used by pedalcycles. [...]

**What it means:** The "highway" is the whole public right-of-way, edge to edge. The "roadway" is only the travel lanes, and expressly excludes the shoulder, berm and sidewalk. That is why § 3545 does not reach a hitchhiker standing on the shoulder.

### 75 Pa.C.S. § 3313: Restrictions on use of limited access highways

**Source:** [Pennsylvania General Assembly, 75 Pa.C.S. § 3313](https://www.palegis.us/statutes/consolidated/view-statute?txtType=HTM&ttl=75&div=0&chapter=33&section=13&subsctn=0)

> (a) General rule.-- The department may regulate or prohibit the use of any limited access highway by any class or kind of traffic which is found to be incompatible with the normal and safe movement of traffic.
>
> (b) Traffic-control devices at entrances.-- The department, when adopting any prohibition under this section, shall erect and maintain official traffic-control devices at the entrances to the limited access highway on which the prohibitions are applicable and when in place no person shall disobey the restrictions stated on the devices.

**What it means:** PennDOT can close a limited access highway to pedestrians, but it does so with signs at the entrances. If the ramp has a "pedestrians prohibited" sign, walking past it is a violation. Stand before the sign.

### 75 Pa.C.S. § 3544: Pedestrians walking along or on highway

**Source:** [Pennsylvania General Assembly, 75 Pa.C.S. § 3544](https://www.palegis.us/statutes/consolidated/view-statute?txtType=HTM&ttl=75&div=0&chapter=35&section=44&subsctn=0)

> (a) Mandatory use of available sidewalk.-- Where a sidewalk is provided and its use is practicable, it is unlawful for any pedestrian to walk along and upon an adjacent roadway.
>
> (b) Absence of sidewalk.-- Where a sidewalk is not available, any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall walk only on a shoulder as far as practicable from the edge of the roadway.
>
> (c) Absence of sidewalk and shoulder.-- Where neither a sidewalk nor a shoulder is available, any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall walk as near as practicable to an outside edge of the roadway and, if on a two-way roadway, shall walk only on the left side of the roadway.

**What it means:** Use the sidewalk if there is one; otherwise the shoulder; otherwise walk on the left edge facing traffic.

### 67 Pa. Code §§ 601.10, 601.11: Pennsylvania Turnpike pedestrian travel and hitchhiking

**Source:** [Pennsylvania Code, 67 Pa. Code Chapter 601 (Turnpike Commission traffic regulations)](https://www.pacodeandbulletin.gov/Display/pacode?file=/secure/pacode/data/067/chapter601/chap601toc.html)

> § 601.10. Pedestrian travel.
>
> Pedestrian travel or entry upon the right-of-way of the Turnpike System is prohibited.
>
> § 601.11. Hitchhiking.
>
> The solicitation for a ride, commonly known as "hitchhiking," is prohibited, and stopping or allowing a vehicle to be standing while hitchhikers board is also prohibited.

From § 601.1 (Definitions):

> Turnpike System—The limited access highway maintained and constructed by the Commission, extending eastward from the Ohio line to the New Jersey line and northward from a point near Norristown, Pennsylvania to a point near Scranton, Pennsylvania and other extensions thereto, which have been or may hereafter be designated as part of the Turnpike System by the Legislature.

**What it means:** On the Turnpike System, you may not walk on the right-of-way at all and you may not hitchhike, and drivers may not stop to pick you up. This includes the shoulders and ramps inside the Turnpike's boundaries.

### 75 Pa.C.S. § 6502 and 67 Pa. Code § 601.16: Penalties

**Source:** [Pennsylvania General Assembly, 75 Pa.C.S. § 6502](https://www.palegis.us/statutes/consolidated/view-statute?txtType=HTM&ttl=75&div=0&chapter=65&section=2&subsctn=0); [67 Pa. Code § 601.16](https://www.pacodeandbulletin.gov/Display/pacode?file=/secure/pacode/data/067/chapter601/chap601toc.html)

> (a) Violations of this title.-- It is a summary offense for any person to violate any of the provisions of this title unless the violation is by this title or other statute of this Commonwealth declared to be a misdemeanor or felony. Every person convicted of a summary offense for a violation of any of the provisions of this title for which another penalty is not provided shall be sentenced to pay a fine of $25.

> § 601.16. Penalties.
>
> A person violating a provision of this part for which no penalty has otherwise been provided by statute is guilty of a summary offense and shall, upon conviction, be sentenced to pay a fine of $25.

**What it means:** Breaking § 3545, § 3544, a § 3313 sign, or the Turnpike rules is a summary offense (the lowest level, like a traffic ticket) with a $25 base fine.

jurisdictions.title: Michigan (US-MI)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Legal. The Michigan Vehicle Code has no statewide ban on soliciting rides. However, the state's model Uniform Traffic Code, which most cities, townships and villages adopt as a local ordinance, bans standing *in the roadway* to solicit a ride. Pedestrians are banned from limited-access highways.

sections.summary:
No section of the Michigan Vehicle Code (Act 300 of 1949) prohibits hitchhiking as such. The ride-soliciting rule lives in the **Uniform Traffic Code for Cities, Townships, and Villages** (Mich. Admin. Code R. 28.1001 et seq.), a model code written by the State Police. It applies only where a city, township or village has adopted it by reference under MCL 257.951. Rule 713 of that code says a person "shall not stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride." "Roadway" takes its Vehicle Code meaning: the part of the highway "used for vehicular travel," which does not include the shoulder.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Never walk onto a freeway** (limited-access highway). MCL 257.679a bans pedestrians there.
- **In most towns, stay out of the travel lanes** when you thumb. Standing on the shoulder or sidewalk is not covered by Rule 713.
- **Don't block or impede traffic** with your body (MCL 257.676b).
- **Walk on the sidewalk where there is one.** Otherwise walk on the left, facing traffic (MCL 257.655).

All of these are civil infractions, not crimes. The fine for a Vehicle Code civil infraction is generally up to $100 plus costs (MCL 257.907).
sections.laws:
### Mich. Comp. Laws § 257.679a: Limited access highway; pedestrians and certain vehicles prohibited

**Source:** [Michigan Legislature, MCL 257.679a](https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-257-679A.pdf) (Michigan Compiled Laws complete through PA 114 of 2026; last amended 1978 PA 510)

> (1) A person shall not operate a motorcycle with less than a 125 cubic centimeter engine, moped, farm tractor, or other self-propelled farm implement, nor shall a pedestrian, bicycle, except as provided in this section, or other nonmotorized traffic be permitted on a limited access highway in this state. Bicycles shall be permitted on paths constructed separately from the roadway and designated for the exclusive use of bicycles.
>
> (2) A person who violates this section is responsible for a civil infraction.

**What it means:** You may not walk on an interstate or other freeway in Michigan, shoulders included. Hitchhike from the surface road before the on-ramp, or from a gas station or truck stop near the interchange.

### Mich. Comp. Laws § 257.26: "Limited access highway" defined

**Source:** [Michigan Legislature, MCL 257.26](https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-257-26.pdf) (unchanged since 1949)

> "Limited access highway" means every highway, street, or roadway in respect to which owners or occupants of abutting lands and other persons have no legal right of access to or from the same except at such points only, and in such manner as may be determined by the public authority having jurisdiction over such highway, street or roadway.

**What it means:** This covers freeways and expressways where you can only get on and off at interchanges.

### Mich. Admin. Code R. 28.1713: Pedestrians; soliciting ride, employment, or business in roadway prohibited (Uniform Traffic Code, Rule 713)

**Source:** [Cornell LII, Mich. Admin. Code R. 28.1713](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-28-1713) (unofficial mirror; history note "1979 AC; 1981 AACS; 2002 AACS")

> (1) A person shall not stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride, employment, or business from the occupant of any vehicle.
>
> (2) A person who violates this rule is responsible for a civil infraction.

**What it means:** Where a city, township or village has adopted the Uniform Traffic Code, don't stand in the travel lanes asking for a ride. The shoulder, curb and sidewalk are not the "roadway" (see MCL 257.55 below), so thumbing from them is not covered by this rule.

### Mich. Admin. Code R. 28.1001: Definitions (Uniform Traffic Code)

**Source:** [Cornell LII, Mich. Admin. Code R. 28.1001](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-28-1001) (unofficial mirror; history note "1979 AC; 1981 AACS; 2002 AACS")

> (2) If any word or phrase used in this code is not defined in this code, but is defined in the Act, PA 300, MCL 257.1 to 257.923, then the definition in the act shall apply to the words and phrases used in this code.

**What it means:** The Uniform Traffic Code borrows the Vehicle Code's definition of "roadway."

### Mich. Comp. Laws § 257.55: "Roadway" defined

**Source:** [Michigan Legislature, MCL 257.55](https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-257-55.pdf) (unchanged since 1949)

> "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel. In the event a highway includes 2 or more separate roadways, the term "roadway", as used herein, shall refer to any such roadway separately, but not to all such roadways collectively.

**What it means:** The roadway is the part cars drive on. The definition doesn't name the shoulder, but a shoulder isn't "ordinarily used for vehicular travel," so standing on it is generally treated as outside the roadway.

### Mich. Comp. Laws § 257.951: Uniform traffic code; adoption by reference

**Source:** [Michigan Legislature, MCL 257.951](https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-257-951.pdf) (Michigan Compiled Laws complete through PA 114 of 2026)

> (1) A city, township, or village may adopt by reference a code or ordinance for the regulation of traffic within cities, townships, and villages that has been promulgated by the director of the department of state police. [...]

**What it means:** Rule 713 is not automatically statewide. It applies inside a city, township or village that has adopted the Uniform Traffic Code, and most have. Assume it applies in town.

### Mich. Comp. Laws § 257.676b: Interference with normal flow of traffic prohibited

**Source:** [Michigan Legislature, MCL 257.676b](https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-257-676B.pdf) (last amended 2021 PA 43)

> (1) Subject to subsection (2), a person, without authority, shall not block, obstruct, impede, or otherwise interfere with the normal flow of vehicular, streetcar, or pedestrian traffic upon a public street or highway in this state, by means of a barricade, object, or device, or with his or her person. [...]
>
> (2) Subsection (1) and any provision of the Michigan Administrative Code that prohibits a person from standing in a roadway other than a limited access highway for the purpose of soliciting a ride, employment, or business from the occupant of any vehicle do not apply to a person who is soliciting contributions on behalf of a charitable or civic organization during daylight hours, if all of the following are satisfied: [...]
>
> (4) A person who violates this section is responsible for a civil infraction.

**What it means:** Don't step out to slow or stop cars. Subsection (2) confirms that the Legislature knows about the Administrative Code ban on standing in a roadway to solicit a ride, and it carves out only charity collectors.

### Mich. Comp. Laws § 257.655: Pedestrians on highways

**Source:** [Michigan Legislature, MCL 257.655](https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-257-655.pdf) (last amended 1978 PA 510)

> (1) Where sidewalks are provided, a pedestrian shall not walk upon the main traveled portion of the highway. Where sidewalks are not provided, pedestrians shall, when practicable, walk on the left side of the highway facing traffic which passes nearest.
>
> (2) A person who violates this section is responsible for a civil infraction.

**What it means:** Use the sidewalk. With no sidewalk, walk on the left side facing oncoming traffic.

### Mich. Comp. Laws § 257.907: Civil infraction fines

**Source:** [Michigan Legislature, MCL 257.907](https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-257-907.pdf) (Michigan Compiled Laws complete through PA 114 of 2026)

> (a) Except as otherwise provided, for a civil infraction under this act or a local ordinance that substantially corresponds to a provision of this act, the person must be ordered to pay a civil fine of not more than $100.00.

**What it means:** Walking on a freeway or blocking traffic gets you a ticket of up to $100 plus court costs, not a criminal record.
sections.unverified-open-questions:
- Rule 713 was quoted from Cornell LII, an unofficial mirror. The official Michigan Administrative Code text (Office of Administrative Hearings and Rules) was not retrieved in this session.
- Which municipalities have adopted the Uniform Traffic Code, and whether any have changed Rule 713 locally, was not checked. Detroit, for example, has its own traffic ordinance.
- Whether MCL 257.679a's ban covers on- and off-ramps isn't stated in the text. Ramps are normally part of the limited-access facility, so treat them as off-limits.

jurisdictions.title: Ohio (US-OH)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not solicit a ride while on the roadway (the travel and parking lanes), but Ohio's definition of "roadway" excludes the berm and shoulder. Pedestrians are banned from freeways, and hitchhiking is banned outright on the Ohio Turnpike.

sections.summary:
Ohio Revised Code § 4511.51(A) says no person "while on a roadway outside a safety zone shall solicit a ride from the driver of any vehicle." Section 4511.01(EE) defines "roadway" as the part of a highway used for vehicle travel and parking lanes, "not including the berm, sidewalk, or shoulder." So thumbing from the sidewalk, curb or shoulder of an ordinary road is not covered by § 4511.51(A).

What still applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stay out of the travel lanes** when you ask for a ride.
- **Don't go onto a freeway at all.** Section 4511.051 bars pedestrians from anywhere within the right-of-way of a freeway, which includes the shoulders, except in a rest area, on a marked pedestrian path, or in an emergency such as a breakdown.
- **The Ohio Turnpike is stricter.** Turnpike Commission rules ban hitchhiking, ban drivers from stopping to pick up or drop off hitchhikers, ban loitering at toll plazas and service plazas, and bar pedestrians from the turnpike.
- **Panhandling-style solicitation is separate.** Section 4511.51(B) bars standing on a highway to solicit "employment, business, or contributions" from vehicle occupants. That division is not about rides.

A first violation of § 4511.51(A) or § 4511.051 is a minor misdemeanor (fine of up to $150). Prior traffic convictions within a year raise it to a fourth- or third-degree misdemeanor.
sections.laws:
### Ohio Rev. Code § 4511.51: Hitchhiking - soliciting employment, business, or contributions from occupant of vehicle

**Source:** [Ohio Laws (Legislative Service Commission), R.C. 4511.51](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-4511.51) (effective January 1, 2004; latest legislation S.B. 123, 124th General Assembly)

> (A) No person while on a roadway outside a safety zone shall solicit a ride from the driver of any vehicle.

**What it means:** Don't stand in the travel lanes (or parking lanes) asking for a ride. Because "roadway" excludes the shoulder and sidewalk (see § 4511.01 below), standing on the shoulder or sidewalk with your thumb out is not covered by this division. A "safety zone" is an officially marked pedestrian island within the roadway.

> (B)(1) Except as provided in division (B)(2) of this section, no person shall stand on a highway for the purpose of soliciting employment, business, or contributions from the occupant of any vehicle.

**What it means:** This bans standing anywhere on a "highway" (which includes the whole right-of-way) to ask drivers for money, work or business. It doesn't mention rides, so it is not a hitchhiking rule. Don't combine a ride request with asking for gas money or donations on a sign.

> (C) No person shall hang onto or ride on the outside of any motor vehicle, streetcar, or trackless trolley while it is moving upon a roadway, [...]
>
> (D) No operator shall knowingly permit any person to hang onto, or ride on the outside of, any motor vehicle, streetcar, or trackless trolley while it is moving upon a roadway, [...]

**What it means:** Ride inside the vehicle. Riding on the outside is illegal for you and for the driver.

> (G)(1) Except as otherwise provided in this division, whoever violates any provision of divisions (A) to (D) of this section is guilty of a minor misdemeanor. If, within one year of the offense, the offender previously has been convicted of or pleaded guilty to one predicate motor vehicle or traffic offense, whoever violates any provision of divisions (A) to (D) of this section is guilty of a misdemeanor of the fourth degree. If, within one year of the offense, the offender previously has been convicted of two or more predicate motor vehicle or traffic offenses, whoever violates any provision of divisions (A) to (D) of this section is guilty of a misdemeanor of the third degree.

**What it means:** A first offense is a minor misdemeanor, the lowest level of offense in Ohio, which carries no jail. Repeat traffic offenses within a year make it a more serious misdemeanor.

### Ohio Rev. Code § 4511.01: Definitions

**Source:** [Ohio Laws (Legislative Service Commission), R.C. 4511.01](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-4511.01) (effective September 30, 2025; latest legislation H.B. 96, 136th General Assembly)

> (BB) "Street" or "highway" means a general term for denoting a public way for purposes of travel by vehicles, streetcars, trackless trolleys, and vulnerable road users, including the entire area within the right-of-way.
>
> [...]
>
> (EE) "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel and parking lanes, not including the berm, sidewalk, or shoulder, even if the berm, sidewalk, or shoulder is used by a person operating a bicycle or other human-powered vehicle. If a highway includes two or more separate roadways the term "roadway" means any such roadway separately but not all such roadways collectively.
>
> [...]
>
> (MM) "Safety zone" means the area or space officially set apart within a roadway for the exclusive use of pedestrians and protected or marked or indicated by adequate signs as to be plainly visible at all times.
>
> [...]
>
> (YY) "Freeway" means a divided multi-lane highway for through traffic with all crossroads separated in grade and with full control of access.

**What it means:** The "roadway" is only the lanes cars drive and park in. The shoulder, berm and sidewalk are not part of it, so the hitchhiking ban in § 4511.51(A) does not reach them. A "highway" is the whole right-of-way, which matters for the freeway ban below.

### Ohio Rev. Code § 4511.051: Freeways - prohibited acts

**Source:** [Ohio Laws (Legislative Service Commission), R.C. 4511.051](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-4511.051) (effective October 29, 2018; latest legislation H.B. 250 and H.B. 95, 132nd General Assembly)

> (A) No person, unless otherwise directed by a police officer, shall:
> (1) As a pedestrian, occupy any space within the limits of the right-of-way of a freeway, except: in a rest area; on a facility that is separated from the roadway and shoulders of the freeway and is designed and appropriately marked for pedestrian use; in the performance of public works or official duties; as a result of an emergency caused by an accident or breakdown of a motor vehicle; or to obtain assistance;
>
> [...]
>
> (B) Except as otherwise provided in this division, whoever violates this section is guilty of a minor misdemeanor. If, within one year of the offense, the offender previously has been convicted of or pleaded guilty to one predicate motor vehicle or traffic offense, whoever violates this section is guilty of a misdemeanor of the fourth degree. If, within one year of the offense, the offender previously has been convicted of two or more predicate motor vehicle or traffic offenses, whoever violates this section is guilty of a misdemeanor of the third degree. [...]

**What it means:** As a pedestrian you may not be anywhere inside a freeway's right-of-way. That covers the shoulders, and ramps are generally inside the freeway right-of-way too (the statute doesn't name ramps, so where the right-of-way begins is a local fact). Rest areas are an exception. Hitchhike from the surface street before the on-ramp, or from a gas station or truck stop near the interchange.

### Ohio Admin. Code 5537-3-02: Hitchhiking and loitering prohibited (Ohio Turnpike)

**Source:** [Ohio Laws, Ohio Administrative Code rule 5537-3-02](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-5537-3-02) (effective March 3, 2001; Ohio Turnpike and Infrastructure Commission)

> The solicitation of a ride, commonly known as "hitchhiking," or stopping for the purpose of picking up or discharging a hitchhiker, is hereby prohibited on the turnpike. Loitering in or about the toll plazas, service plazas or any other portion of the turnpike is prohibited.

**What it means:** On the Ohio Turnpike (I-80/I-90 across northern Ohio), hitchhiking is banned everywhere, including service plazas and toll plazas. Drivers are also forbidden to stop to pick you up or drop you off. Asking for rides at turnpike service plazas can get you cited.

### Ohio Admin. Code 5537-3-01: Prohibited users (Ohio Turnpike)

**Source:** [Ohio Laws, Ohio Administrative Code rule 5537-3-01](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-5537-3-01) (effective September 1, 2023)

> The following shall not be permitted to travel on the turnpike: (A) Pedestrians. (B) Bicycles. [...]

**What it means:** You may not walk on the turnpike.

### Ohio Rev. Code §§ 5537.16(C) and 5537.99: Penalty for violating turnpike rules

**Source:** [R.C. 5537.16](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-5537.16) (effective March 23, 2022) and [R.C. 5537.99](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-5537.99) (effective July 1, 2009), Ohio Laws

> (C) No person shall violate any such bylaws or rules of the commission.

> (A) Except as provided in division (B) of this section, whoever violates division (C) of section 5537.16 of the Revised Code is guilty of a minor misdemeanor on a first offense; on each subsequent offense such person is guilty of a misdemeanor of the fourth degree.

**What it means:** Breaking the turnpike hitchhiking rule is a minor misdemeanor the first time, and a fourth-degree misdemeanor after that. This applies to drivers who stop for you, too.

### Ohio Rev. Code § 2929.28: Financial sanctions for misdemeanors

**Source:** [Ohio Laws, R.C. 2929.28](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-2929.28) (effective October 3, 2023)

> (iv) For a misdemeanor of the fourth degree, not more than two hundred fifty dollars;
> (v) For a minor misdemeanor, not more than one hundred fifty dollars.

**What it means:** The maximum fine for a minor misdemeanor is $150, and $250 for a fourth-degree misdemeanor, plus court costs.

jurisdictions.title: Utah (US-UT)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Legal. No Utah statute currently prohibits soliciting a ride. Walking on no-access freeways is prohibited, and you may not impede or block traffic on interstates, freeways, state highways, or fast roads.

sections.summary:
Utah no longer has a statewide ban on hitchhiking. Before 2017, Utah Code § 41-6a-1009(4) listed "soliciting rides, contributions, or other business" as conduct that may impede or block traffic. The 2017 General Session (H.B. 161, "Pedestrian Safety Amendments") struck that wording. The section now targets handing money or property between pedestrians and occupants of moving traffic.

What still applies to hitchhikers:

- **Don't walk on no-access freeways** (interstates and other limited-access highways) unless there is an emergency. Stand at the on-ramp, before the freeway begins.
- **Don't impede or block traffic** on interstates, freeways, state highways or routes, or highways that are paved with a speed limit of 35 mph or more, that have a median, or that share the right-of-way with a railway. This includes shoulders, on-ramps, off-ramps and medians.
- **Walk on the sidewalk** if there is one. Otherwise walk on the shoulder, or on the left edge facing traffic.
- **Cities and counties may add their own rules** for the locations listed in subsection (4).

A violation is an infraction. A third violation of subsection (4) within one year is a class C misdemeanor.
sections.laws:
### Utah Code § 41-6a-1009: Use of roadway by pedestrians -- Prohibited activities

**Source:** [Utah Legislature, Utah Code § 41-6a-1009](https://le.utah.gov/xcode/Title41/Chapter6A/41-6a-S1009.html) (version effective 5/8/2018, amended by Chapter 122, 2018 General Session)

> (1) Where there is a sidewalk provided and its use is practicable, a pedestrian may not walk along or on an adjacent roadway.
>
> (2) Where a sidewalk is not provided, a pedestrian walking along or on a highway shall walk only on the shoulder, as far as practicable from the edge of the roadway.
>
> (3) Where a sidewalk or a shoulder is not available, a pedestrian walking along or on a highway shall:
> (a) walk as near as practicable to the outside edge of the roadway; and
> (b) if on a two-way roadway, walk only on the left side of the roadway facing traffic.

**What it means:** If there is a sidewalk, walk on it. If there isn't one, walk on the shoulder. If there's no shoulder, walk on the left side of the road facing traffic.

> (4)(a) An individual may not impede or block traffic within any of the following:
> (i) an interstate system, as defined in Section 72-1-102;
> (ii) a freeway, as defined in Section 41-6a-102;
> (iii) a state highway, as defined in Title 72, Chapter 4, Designation of State Highways Act;
> (iv) a state route, or "SR," as defined in Section 72-1-102; or
> (v) a highway, as defined in Section 72-1-102, that:
> (A) is paved and has a speed limit of 35 miles per hour or higher;
> (B) has a median, whether elevated or flat; or
> (C) has a fixed guideway as defined in Section 59-12-102 or any other railway that shares the highway right-of-way.
>
> (b) The locations described in Subsection (4)(a) include:
> (i) shoulder areas, as defined in Section 41-6a-102;
> (ii) on-ramps;
> (iii) off-ramps; and
> (iv) an area between the roadways of a divided highway, as defined in Section 41-6a-102.
>
> (c) The locations described in Subsection (4)(a) do not include sidewalks, as defined in Section 41-6a-102.
>
> (d) Conduct that may impede or block traffic includes:
> (i) while a pedestrian, accepting, transacting, exchanging, or otherwise taking possession or control of money or property from a person within a motor vehicle while that motor vehicle is within an area described in Subsection (4)(a); [...]
>
> (f) A county or municipality may adopt a resolution, ordinance, or regulation prohibiting conduct in locations described in Subsections (4)(a) and (b) within any of the roadways under its jurisdiction.

**What it means:** Standing on a shoulder or ramp with your thumb out is not listed as prohibited conduct. Stepping into traffic or making cars stop in a travel lane is. Pick a spot where a driver can pull completely off the road. Local ordinances can be stricter (see (4)(f)), so check city rules in places like Salt Lake City.

> (7) A pedestrian may not walk along or on a no-access freeway facility except during an emergency.

**What it means:** Don't walk on interstates or other limited-access freeways. Hitchhike from the on-ramp entrance or a nearby gas station, not from the freeway shoulder.

> (9)(a) Except as provided in Subsection (9)(b), a violation of this section is an infraction.
> (b) A third or subsequent violation of Subsection (4) in a one-year period is a class C misdemeanor.

**What it means:** A first or second violation is an infraction, which carries a fine and no jail. Repeat violations of the traffic-blocking rule within a year become a class C misdemeanor.
sections.history:
### 2017 H.B. 161: "soliciting rides" removed

**Source:** [Utah Legislature, 2017 H.B. 161 (enrolled), Pedestrian Safety Amendments](https://le.utah.gov/~2017/bills/hbillenr/HB0161.htm)

Before this bill, § 41-6a-1009(4)(d) read: "Conduct that impedes or blocks traffic may include: (i) loitering; (ii) demonstrating or picketing; (iii) distributing materials; (iv) gathering signatures; (v) holding signs; or (vi) soliciting rides, contributions, or other business." The bill struck that whole list and replaced it with the money and property exchange language quoted above.

**What it means:** Older guides that say "Utah bans soliciting rides on highways" describe the pre-2017 law.
